html:
The Mossi Kingdoms were a group of states in the basin of the Volta rivers, in what is now Burkina Faso, shown on the map from 1492 to 1900. The Mossi are still the largest people of Burkina Faso, about half its population.

Tradition traces the founding dynasty to the princess Yennenga and riders from the Dagomba lands to the south. The main kingdoms were Ouagadougou, ruled by the Mogho Naba, Yatenga to the north, Tenkodogo and Fada N'Gourma. They were horse-riding warrior states with elaborate courts, and they kept their own religion for centuries while their neighbours turned to Islam.

The Mossi raided the Niger bend and clashed with the Mali and Songhai empires. Askia Muhammad I of Songhai declared a holy war on them in the 1490s, but the kingdoms survived and outlasted Songhai itself.

France conquered Ouagadougou in 1896 and made the region part of Upper Volta, which became independent in 1960 and was renamed Burkina Faso in 1984. The Mogho Naba still holds a ceremonial role today.
